blocks.text: Qohelet presents a royal-scale experiment: pleasure, wine, building, gardens, wealth, music, and labor are all tested, yet none provides lasting “profit.” The royal persona is not named Solomon in Ecclesiastes itself. Wisdom remains preferable to folly, like light to darkness, but it cannot prevent the shared fate of death or secure lasting remembrance; achievement must also be left to another person. This gives force to “vanity” or “striving after wind”: the image of vapor can suggest transience, frustration, enigma, or an absurd mismatch between effort and outcome, rather than one single fixed idea. The chapter nevertheless ends by commending eating, drinking, and finding enjoyment in work as a person’s portion, received from God amid conditions people cannot control.
